title: Queen Helena

Queen Helena
This text presents a comprehensive analysis of the kingdom of Adiabene in the first century CE, focusing on the figure of Queen Helena and her decisive influence on Jerusalem in the Second Temple period. The study surveys the royal family's passage from the Parthian Empire into the fold of Judaism, examining the tension between spiritual motives and geopolitical strategies intended to strengthen ties with the Jewish communities of the East. On the practical plane, the article highlights Helena's royal philanthropy, which included saving the inhabitants of Jerusalem from famine and magnificent technological gifts to the Temple, alongside an uncompromising religious strictness reflected in the literature of the Sages. Finally, the source draws on impressive archaeological finds, such as her palaces in the City of David and the "Tombs of the Kings" burial estate, to illustrate the physical and cultural presence of the queen as a living bridge between the powers of the East and the spiritual center in Judea.
The Philanthropy, Government and Religious Teaching of Queen Helena: A Multidisciplinary Analysis of the Kingdom of Adiabene in First-Century CE Jerusalem
Introduction and the Geopolitical Framework of the Kingdom of Adiabene
The rise of Queen Helena and the kingdom of Adiabene onto the stage of Jewish history in the first century CE constitutes one of the most complex and influential chapters in the history of the Second Temple period. Helena, a figure admired both in external historical sources and in the literature of the Sages, represents the link between the Parthian Empire in the East and the spiritual and political center in Jerusalem.[1, 2, 3] The kingdom of Adiabene, which lay in the region of northern Mesopotamia (identified today with the region of Kurdistan and Iraq), was a vassal entity under the protection of the Parthian Empire, and its strategic location made it a cultural and economic crossroads.[2, 3]
Helena was the sister and wife of King Monobaz Bazeus, as was the custom of the royal dynasties of the Mesopotamian region at that time.[2, 3] Of this marriage her son was born, King Izates II, whose figure is closely bound up with the conversion of the whole family. The historical record of Queen Helena has been preserved along two main paths: the first is the historical-political narrative of Josephus (Yosef ben Matityahu), and the second is the collective, halakhic memory of the sages of the Mishnah and the Talmud.[2, 3, 4] Whereas Josephus focuses on the diplomatic and personal motives of the royal family, the Sages extol her personal piety, her generosity and her deep integration into the world of Pharisaic halakha.[1, 2, 4]
Modern analysis of the period indicates that the kingdom of Adiabene's joining of Judaism was not an isolated religious event but part of a broad geopolitical trend. In the first century, the Jewish communities of the eastern diaspora constituted a significant economic and political force.[3, 5] Queen Helena, through her activity in Jerusalem, created a bridge between the empires and made the capital of Judea a political center for sovereign entities in the East, which had far-reaching consequences for relations with the ruling Roman Empire.[3]
Basic Data on the Kingdom of Adiabene and the Royal House
The Process of Conversion: Between Spiritual Teaching and Political Strategy
The conversion of Helena and her sons is described in the writings of Josephus as a twofold event that took place simultaneously at the royal court in Adiabene and in the port of Charax Spasinou.[2, 3] While Prince Izates was staying at the king's court in this port, he met a Jewish merchant named Hananiah (Ananias), who drew him close to the Torah of Israel.[2, 8] At the same time and independently, Queen Helena was guided in the ways of Judaism by another Jew in Adiabene.[2, 8]
The narrative of the conversion reveals a deep inner tension between the religious and the political levels. When Izates sought to circumcise himself in order to become a "complete" Jew, Helena expressed grave concern.[4, 8] She argued that the subjects of the kingdom would not agree to be ruled by a king who observes "foreign customs," and that this could lead to rebellion.[8] Hananiah the merchant, who represented a pragmatic approach, supported Helena's position and ruled that one may worship God even without circumcision if the political circumstances require it.[4, 8] However, the appearance of a Galilean sage named Elazar changed the picture; Elazar insisted that reading the Torah without fulfilling its practical commandments, and especially the covenant of circumcision, is an unforgivable sin.[4, 8] In the end, Izates chose the stricter path, and Helena's backing of this step marked Adiabene's transformation into a declared Jewish kingdom.[1, 2, 8]
Beyond the spiritual aspect, scholars such as Jacob Neusner suggest that the conversion was part of a calculated political move.[3] The Jewish community in Babylonia and Mesopotamia was a military and political force that could not be ignored. By adopting Judaism, the royal family of Adiabene could form a strategic alliance with the Jews of the Land of Israel and with the wealthy communities of the East, thereby strengthening its position vis-à-vis both the Roman and the Parthian empires.[3] This action paralleled earlier attempts by King Herod to form ties with Babylonian Jewry, but Helena and her sons went one step further and fully converted.[3]
Queen Helena's Philanthropy in Jerusalem: Crisis Management in the First Century
In the 40s of the first century CE, Queen Helena came to Jerusalem on a visit that turned into a prolonged stay.[3, 4] Her pilgrimage was not only a religious act of prostration at the Temple, but a move that made her the central figure in the city's system of relief and welfare.[2, 9] At that time a severe famine struck Judea (apparently in the days of the emperor Claudius, around 45–48 CE), and the local population faced the danger of annihilation.[2, 3, 6]
Helena's response to the crisis was swift and wide-ranging. She set her royal logistical apparatus in motion to purchase enormous quantities of wheat from Egypt and dried figs from Cyprus.[2, 3, 6, 9] This food was brought to Jerusalem and distributed to the poor free of charge. Her son, King Izates, supported her efforts and sent enormous sums of money to the community leaders in Jerusalem to help rehabilitate the city.[3, 9] These actions established Helena's standing as the adoptive "mother of the nation," and Josephus notes that her deeds left her an everlasting name that would endure for generations.[9]
Helena's philanthropy reveals a consolidated "social teaching." She saw her royal wealth as a means of realizing the Jewish values of charity and mutual responsibility.[2] In doing so, she not only supplied food but also strengthened the legitimacy of her rule and of her conversion in the eyes of the people in Jerusalem. This influence was so strong that the sages of the Mishnah saw fit to mention the royal family of Adiabene alongside the greatest donors to the Temple.[1, 10]
Queen Helena's Gifts to the Second Temple: Technology, Worship and Halakha
In the Mishnah, in tractate Yoma (3:10), Helena and her son Monobaz are mentioned with praise for their magnificent and unique gifts to the Temple.[1, 10] These gifts were not merely an expression of wealth but were intended to solve real halakhic and ritual problems, using technology that was advanced for its time.[10, 11]
The Golden Chandelier and the Marking of the Time for the Recitation of Shema
Helena donated a huge golden chandelier that was placed above the entrance to the Sanctuary.[10, 11] The main function of the chandelier was to serve as an instrument for measuring halakhic time precisely. When the sun rose in the east, its rays would strike the chandelier hanging in the west (above the entrance to the Sanctuary), and the reflection of the polished gold would produce "sparks" or "rays of splendor" that were visible throughout Jerusalem.[10, 11]
This optical mechanism allowed the city's inhabitants to know the exact moment when the time for the morning recitation of Shema had arrived, even before the sun lit up the city's narrow streets.[10, 11] The discussion in the Jerusalem Talmud raises various possibilities as to its form: a lamp, a polished tablet, or a round ornament ("konbita") whose purpose was to reflect light.[11] Either way, the gift testifies to Helena's desire to integrate her faith into the public and daily life of Jerusalem.[10]
The Golden Tablet of the Sotah Passage
Another unique gift was a golden tablet on which the passage of the sotah was written.[2, 3, 10, 12] The purpose was practical and halakhic: in the sotah ritual, the priest had to write the passage on a scroll and blot it out in water.[12, 13] So that they would not need to bring out a complete Torah scroll each time (something that involved trouble and the risk of disrespect to the scroll), Helena donated a permanent tablet that served as an accessible reference text for copying.[10, 12]
The Talmud, in tractate Gittin, discusses this gift in the context of the question whether it is permitted to write portions of the Torah separately.[12] The very fact that this gift was accepted in the Temple served as proof that the Sages viewed Helena's actions favorably, and that she acted in full accordance with the halakhic tradition they accepted.[12]
Comparison of the Gifts of the Royal House of Adiabene to the Temple
The investment of Helena and Monobaz in gold for the Temple is not merely an expression of wealth but a declaration of absolute loyalty to the service of God in Jerusalem. They chose to invest in objects that made the religious service more efficient, and thereby became active partners in the running of the Temple.[1, 4, 10]
Helena's Religious and Halakhic Teaching: Nazirite Vows, the Sukkah and the Approach of the House of Shammai
Queen Helena did not content herself with the outward activity of gifts and building, but adopted a strict religious way of life that prompted central halakhic discussions among the Tannaim. She emerges as a woman of deep religious awareness, inclined at times to be stricter with herself than required.[1, 4]
A Nazirite Vow of 21 Years: Perseverance and Obedience to the Sages
The sources relate that Helena vowed to be a nazirite for seven years if her son returned safely from war.[1, 4] After her son returned and she had completed the period outside the Land, she went up to the Land of Israel.[1] Here a halakhic question arose: the House of Hillel ruled that a nazirite period observed outside the Land does not count with regard to the offering of the sacrifices, and that she must therefore observe seven more years in the Land of Israel.[1, 4]
Toward the end of the second seven years, Helena became impure through contact with the dead, which by law required her to cancel all the days of her naziriteship and begin anew.[1, 4] As a result, she had to observe another seven years, and in all she was a nazirite for 21 years (and some opinions reduce this to 14 years).[1, 3, 4] Her devotion to the nazirite vow despite the difficulties made her a symbol of the "righteous convert" (giyoret tzedek) who takes upon herself the yoke of the commandments and the authority of the Sages without question.[1]
Helena's Tall Sukkah and the Discussion of a Woman's Authority
Another halakhic event associated with Helena is the sukkah she erected, which was taller than twenty cubits.[1, 14, 15] According to the opinion of the Sages in the Mishnah, such a sukkah is invalid, but Rabbi Yehuda declares it valid and brings as proof the sukkah of Helena, which the Sages visited without objecting to it.[1, 15]
The Talmud, in tractate Sukkah, describes a highly complex sukkah that had "chambers upon chambers" (kitoniyot kitoniyot): inner rooms and separate spaces.[14] The queen sat in the inner rooms for reasons of modesty, while her sons, who were described as Torah scholars, sat in the central space of the sukkah.[1, 14] The case of Helena's sukkah teaches about her high standing: she was so significant that her actions served as a legal precedent in the deliberations of the Sanhedrin concerning the laws of the sukkah.[1, 15] Scholars such as Tal Ilan have raised the possibility that Helena inclined toward the approach of the House of Shammai, known for its stricter and more rigid approach, which may explain the length of her naziriteship and the features of her sukkah.[2]
Queen Helena's Palaces in Jerusalem: Architecture as an Instrument of Government
Helena's activity in Jerusalem included the construction of magnificent public and residential buildings that changed the skyline of the Lower City. Josephus notes that Helena built three main palaces: for herself, for her son Monobaz, and for her mother-in-law.[16] These palaces were located in the area of the "Ophel," the area connecting the City of David with the Temple.[1, 4, 9]
The Finds at the Givati Parking Lot
In extensive archaeological excavations conducted at the Givati Parking Lot under the direction of Dr. Doron Ben-Ami and Yana Tchekhanovets, remains were uncovered of a monumental building that many scholars today identify as the palace of Queen Helena.[4, 9, 17, 18] The building is an architectural exception in the relatively modest building landscape of the Lower City at the end of the Second Temple period.[9, 16]
Features of the archaeological structure:
Massive walls: the walls of the building were built of heavy ashlar stones, some weighing hundreds of kilograms, and their thickness exceeded one meter.[9, 16, 19]
A basement floor and arches: foundations were found of a basement floor supported by rows of massive arches (vaults), intended to bear the weight of several stories above them.[9, 19]
Decorations and frescoes: on the remains of the walls, colored plaster and wall paintings (frescoes) with plant and geometric patterns were found, similar in style to the palaces of King Herod at Masada and Jericho.[9, 19]
Ritual baths: in the northern part of the building, two large ritual baths (mikvaot) and a storage pool were uncovered, attesting to particular care for the laws of purity among the palace's residents.[9, 19]
The palace was apparently destroyed in 70 CE during the Roman siege, as attested by the huge collapsed stones found on the floors and the signs of burning at the site.[4, 16, 19] The identification of the building as Helena's palace rests on the precise location given by Josephus and on the fact that it is the only monumental building of its kind found south of the Temple Mount in the area of the Lower City.[9, 16]
The Tombs of the Kings: The Monumental Burial Estate North of Jerusalem
The most famous and best-preserved architectural undertaking associated with Queen Helena is the burial estate known as the "Tombs of the Kings."[6, 7] The site, which lies north of the wall of Jerusalem (in the area of today's Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood), is considered the most magnificent burial site from the Second Temple period in the Land of Israel.[2, 6, 7, 20]
The Structure of the Site and Its Engineering Design
The burial estate is hewn entirely into the bedrock and extends over a wide area. It was designed as a family memorial site for Helena and her sons, and combines architectural elements from both the Hellenistic and the Jewish world.[6, 7]
Components of the estate:
The entrance courtyard and the staircase: a wide staircase (9 meters) descends to the tomb, leading to a spacious inner courtyard (27X25 meters).[7] The steps include channels for draining rainwater that feed ritual baths hewn at their foot.[7]
The decorated façade (the distylos): the façade of the cave was adorned with rich plant reliefs including clusters of grapes, acanthus leaves, pine cones and pomegranates.[6, 7] Originally two columns with Ionic capitals stood in the façade, supporting the decorated frieze.[6, 7, 9]
The pyramids (the funerary monuments): the historical sources mention three pyramids that stood above the façade of the tomb.[2, 6, 7, 20] Scholars believe that these were not "classical" pyramids as in Egypt, but structures with a shaped conical roof, similar to the roof of Absalom's Monument (Yad Avshalom).[6, 7, 20]
The rolling stone and the secret mechanism: the entrance to the cave was sealed with a large round rolling stone. Pausanias, a Greek traveler of the 2nd century, tells of a secret mechanical mechanism that opened the stone at fixed times, a description that attests to the engineering complexity of the site.[6, 7]
The "Tzadan Malkata" Sarcophagus and the Proof of the Burial
In 1863 the French archaeologist Félicien de Saulcy discovered a sarcophagus (a stone coffin) in one of the chambers of the cave.[7, 9] On the coffin was engraved an inscription in two languages (Aramaic and Syriac): "Tzadan Malkata" / "Tzada Malkatah."[2, 7, 20] This discovery constituted unequivocal proof of the identity of those buried at the site.
Scholars believe that "Tzadan" was the queen's original name in the language of her country (Adiabene), whereas "Helena" was her Greek name by which she was known in the Mediterranean world.[2, 7, 20] The coffin, decorated with delicate reliefs of the fruits of the land, is today in the Louvre Museum, and it is tangible evidence of the deep bond between the royal house of Adiabene and Jerusalem.[2, 7]
Comparison of the Features of the Tombs of the Kings Site with Other Burial Sites
The Geopolitical Aspect: Adiabene as a Bridge between Parthia and Rome
The conversion of the kingdom of Adiabene and its transformation into an ally of Jerusalem were not merely religious events, but moves that shook the diplomatic system of the Near East. Adiabene lay at the very heart of the Parthian Empire, Rome's sworn enemy.[2, 3]
The historian Jacob Neusner argues that Helena and Izates in effect created a "third option" in the region.[3] By adopting Judaism, they bound their fate to the large Jewish communities in Babylonia and Judea, and thereby created a political force that could challenge Roman control in the East.[3] This fact explains why members of the royal family of Adiabene took an active part in the Great Revolt against Rome (66–70 CE). Josephus mentions that relatives of King Monobaz displayed extraordinary valor in the battles against the Tenth Legion, and some of them were even taken as hostages to Rome after the destruction.[5, 6]
Queen Helena, through her activity in Jerusalem, in effect served as an "ambassador" of the Jewish East in the capital of Judea. She built palaces not only as residences but as diplomatic centers of power intended to display the presence of Adiabene at the heart of the Jewish religious center.[3, 4]
Helena's Legacy and Teaching: Summary and Integrative Analysis
The teaching of Queen Helena, as it emerges from the sources, is a teaching of "universal Judaism" and total commitment. She did not regard her Judaism as a cultural ornament, but as a demanding way of life requiring personal sacrifice and deep social involvement.
The value of giving and the responsibility of government: Helena used her royal resources to save Jerusalem from famine. She set a model of "serving government," in which royal wealth is meant to serve the needs of the people in a time of crisis.[2, 9]
Integration into halakha and acceptance of the authority of the Sages: despite her high standing as a sovereign queen, Helena submitted to the rulings of the sages of Jerusalem, as seen in the cases of the nazirite vow and the sukkah.[1, 4] She chose to integrate into the mainstream of Pharisaic Judaism rather than create a separate "royal Judaism."
Loyalty to Jerusalem as a spiritual center: the fact that Helena built her palaces and her tomb in Jerusalem, although her kingdom was hundreds of kilometers away, testifies to a worldview that saw Zion as the exclusive center of her identity.[3, 5, 6]
The legacy of Queen Helena continued to resonate through the generations. In early Syriac Christianity, her story served as an inspiration for stories of the conversion of kings to Christianity, while preserving her image as a model of female piety.[5] In modern Judaism, she remains a symbol of the "righteous convert" who gave the Jewish people her all, and thus became an inseparable part of the history and architecture of Jerusalem.[3, 21]
Helena's story is a testimony to the attractive power of Judaism in the first century, and to the potential inherent in the bond between political power and religious and social values. She was not merely the queen of a distant land, but became a queen who lives at the very heart of the alleys of Jerusalem and in the pages of Jewish history and halakha to this day.
